UNE COM · Medical Neuroanatomy Spinal Cord Application Session
6 cases · case-based localization
Overview Case 1 · Brown-Séquard Case 2 · Epidural Abscess Case 3 · Incidental Syrinx Case 4 · Syringobulbia Case 5 · Wallerian Degeneration Case 6 · Wallenberg Syndrome Gallery
Overview

How to Work Through These Cases

This session is six real spinal-cord/brainstem cases used to practice a single repeatable workflow: figure out where the lesion is (which tracts, which side, which level) before you guess what it is. Two axes matter every time:

1. Transverse localization

Which tract is knocked out tells you which side of the cord and which functional system — motor (lateral corticospinal), proprioception/vibration (dorsal columns), or pain/temperature (spinothalamic).

2. Longitudinal localization

The sensory/motor "level" tells you how high or low the lesion sits along the neuraxis. A sharply demarcated level favors a discrete cord lesion; a length-dependent "stocking" pattern favors peripheral nerve.

Cord Transection — Differential Framework

Once you know a lesion is transecting the cord (partially or completely), the tempo of onset plus the clinical context narrows the etiology fast:

CategoryExampleTypical Tempo
TraumaticPenetrating injury, fracture-dislocation, contusionSeconds–minutes
DegenerativeSpinal stenosisMonths–years
NeoplasticMass effect from primary or metastatic tumorWeeks–months
InfectiousEpidural abscess (mass effect + vascular compromise)Hours–days
AutoimmuneTransverse myelitisHours–days
VascularAnterior spinal artery (ASA) infarctionMinutes–hours
CongenitalSpina bifida (and tethering/syrinx it predisposes to)Present from birth; symptoms may emerge later

The Six Cases at a Glance

  • Case 1 — Stab wound, left neckBrown-Séquard (cord hemisection) syndrome
  • Case 2 — 21-year-old with back painSpinal epidural abscess (Staph. aureus)
  • Case 3 — Skydiving instructor, midthoracic painIncidental, asymptomatic syrinx
  • Case 4 — Progressive arm wasting, dysphonia, dysphagiaSyringobulbia / syringomyelia
  • Case 5 — Fatal tobogganing injuryWallerian degeneration above & below a cord transection
  • Case 6 — Near-drowning, hyperextended neckVertebral artery dissection → lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome
Case 1

Stab Wound to the Neck → Brown-Séquard Syndrome

Vignette

A 21-year-old man presented with a stab wound to the left side of the neck.

Clinical Photo Entry wound just below and behind the ear on the left lateral neck.

Exam Findings

➡️
Right side
Sensory level at C5
Proprioception / vibration (dorsal column) deficit
⬅️
Left side
Pin-prick loss from C7 down
Pain / temperature (spinothalamic) deficit
➡️
Right side
Hemiplegia
Corticospinal (motor) deficit
⬅️
Left side
Sensory loss in the foot
Same contralateral pain/temp column, extending caudally
⚠️ Don't anchor on the wound side

The knife entered the left neck, but every ipsilateral finding (dorsal column loss, hemiplegia) is on the right. Localize strictly from the exam pattern, not from where the skin was cut — the blade's internal trajectory, not the entry point, determines which half of the cord is hemisected. Here the findings triangulate to a right hemicord lesion at approximately C5.

Why the Pattern Looks Like This

A lateral hemisection of the cord (Brown-Séquard syndrome) knocks out three long tracts, and each one produces a different "which side, which level" signature because of where it crosses:

TractCarriesWhere it crossesDeficit relative to lesion
Dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis/cuneatus)Proprioception, vibration, fine touchLow medulla (internal arcuate fibers)Ipsilateral loss, at the level of the lesion
Lateral corticospinal tractVoluntary motorAlready crossed at the pyramidal decussationIpsilateral weakness, at/below the lesion
Lateral spinothalamic tractPain, temperatureAnterior white commissure, 1–2 segments above cell of originContralateral loss, beginning 1–2 levels below the lesion

That 1–2 segment lag is exactly why the right-sided (ipsilateral) dorsal column level sits at C5 while the left-sided (contralateral) pain/temperature level doesn't start until C7 — the crossing spinothalamic fibers near the lesion haven't decussated yet, so a thin band of sparing sits right at the lesion level.

Imaging

Sagittal MRICervical spine, arrow marking the cord signal abnormality at the injury level.
Axial MRICross-section through the injury; arrows mark the hemicord contusion.
SchematicCross-section of a lateral cord hemisection — pale (light) hemicord = the injured, non-conducting side.

Reference Tract Diagrams

These three classic diagrams are the ones to have memorized cold — every hemicord/level question comes back to tracing one of these three columns from periphery to cortex (or cortex to periphery).

Corticospinal TractMotor cortex → internal capsule → crus cerebri → pyramid → pyramidal decussation → lateral corticospinal tract → anterior horn cell.
Dorsal Column–Medial LemniscusFasciculus gracilis/cuneatus → nucleus gracilis/cuneatus → internal arcuate fibers cross in the medulla → medial lemniscus → thalamus.
Anterolateral (Spinothalamic) SystemDorsal root → Lissauer's tract → substantia gelatinosa → crosses in the ventral white commissure within 1–2 levels → ascends as the lateral spinothalamic tract.
💡 High-yield takeaway

Brown-Séquard = ipsilateral motor + ipsilateral proprioception/vibration below the lesion, with contralateral pain/temperature loss beginning a couple of segments below that. If a question gives you a clean split like this, the diagnosis is the hemisection itself — the exam question is really testing whether you can trace the three columns.

Case 2

21-Year-Old with Back Pain → Spinal Epidural Abscess

Vignette — Presentation

A 21-year-old male presented to the ED in Portland with back pain. CT was negative. Over the next 1.5 hours he began losing power in the lower extremities — ankle before knee before hip — accompanied by a progressive "stocking-like" sensory loss below the knees.

Audience Question 1

Which of the following could be ruled out at this point?

  1. Guillain-Barré syndrome
  2. CMT neuropathy
  3. Intramedullary spinal mass
  4. Extramedullary spinal mass
  5. Anterior spinal artery infarction
  6. Syringomyelia
  7. Multiple sclerosis
  8. Herniated disc
Reasoning: the pace is the clue. Onset and progression over 1.5 hours is far too fast for CMT neuropathy (an inherited, slowly progressive polyneuropathy over years) or classic syringomyelia (typically progresses over months). Both can reasonably be set aside for now; a discrete cord lesion, acute demyelination, vascular event, or rapidly expanding mass are all still on the table.
Vignette — 2 Hours In

By 2 hours after admission he had lost control of bladder and bowel. By 3 hours he had developed a sharply demarcated sensory level at T10. A medical procedure was performed.

Audience Question 2

Which of the following could now be ruled out?

  1. Guillain-Barré syndrome
  2. CMT neuropathy
  3. Intramedullary spinal mass
  4. Extramedullary spinal mass
  5. Anterior spinal artery infarction
  6. Syringomyelia
  7. Multiple sclerosis
  8. Herniated disc
Reasoning: a sharply demarcated sensory level is a cord-level (myelopathic) finding, not a peripheral one. Guillain-Barré is a peripheral polyradiculoneuropathy — it produces an ascending, length-dependent deficit, never a crisp dermatomal level. That makes Guillain-Barré syndrome the one to drop here. Bladder/bowel involvement plus a discrete level both point straight at the spinal cord itself.
Vignette — Lumbar Puncture

The LP (the "medical procedure" above) showed normal opening pressure with normal respiratory fluctuation, normal protein, and no measurable glucose.

Audience Question 3

Which of the following could now be ruled out?

  1. Guillain-Barré syndrome
  2. CMT neuropathy
  3. Intramedullary spinal mass
  4. Extramedullary spinal mass
  5. Anterior spinal artery infarction
  6. Syringomyelia
  7. Multiple sclerosis
  8. Herniated disc
Reasoning: two CSF clues matter. Normal pressure with preserved respiratory fluctuation argues against a complete subarachnoid block from a large compressive mass (a complete block classically flattens that fluctuation and drives protein way up — Froin's pattern). Essentially no glucose in the CSF (hypoglycorrhachia) is the bigger red flag — organisms consuming glucose points hard toward an infectious process, and doesn't fit a purely mechanical problem like a herniated disc or a demyelinating one like multiple sclerosis.
Audience Question 4

Now what do you want?

  1. MRI
  2. CT without contrast
  3. CT with contrast
  4. PET scan
  5. Nerve conduction velocity (NCV)
Reasoning: MRI — it is the gold standard for cord and epidural-space pathology, with far better soft-tissue resolution than CT for detecting an abscess, cord edema, or compression. PET is not an acute tool, and NCV interrogates peripheral nerve, not the cord.

Imaging Series

The imaging obtained in this case (from the "DDX Case 31" teaching set) — a sagittal scout localizer followed by a sequential axial series through the lesion:

Series 08Representative image from the diagnostic series.
Scout / LocalizerSagittal localizer showing the level of the epidural collection.
Axial 00Axial slice through the spinal canal.
Axial 01Sequential axial slice.
Axial 02Sequential axial slice — epidural collection compressing the thecal sac.
Axial 03Sequential axial slice.
Axial 05Sequential axial slice.
Axial 07Final axial slice in the series.
Audience Question 5

The differential diagnosis of a "mass" on this imaging includes which of the following?

  1. Tumor
  2. Abscess
  3. MS plaque
  4. Herniated disc
Reasoning: all four. Each of these can present as a discrete mass-like lesion compressing the cord/canal on imaging — this question is testing breadth of the mass differential, not elimination.
Diagnosis Spinal cord compression secondary to Staph. aureus epidural abscess

Rapidly progressive myelopathy + fever risk + hypoglycorrhachia + a compressive epidural collection = surgical emergency. Epidural abscess is a decompress-and-culture diagnosis; delay costs cord function.

Epidural Abscess — Location, Mechanism, Risk Factors

Distribution by LevelEpidural abscesses are more often posterior than anterior, and most common in the thoracic region — reflecting the anatomy of the posterior epidural fat and venous plexus.Chao D & Nanda A. Am Fam Physician 2002;65:1341–1346.
Compression MechanismPus collects in the epidural fat around the posterior spinal arteries and venous plexus, compressing the cord directly and compromising its blood supply.Chao D & Nanda A. Am Fam Physician 2002;65:1341–1346.
⚠️ Clinical pearl

Cord injury in epidural abscess is not just mechanical — direct compression plus venous congestion/arterial compromise both contribute, which is why deficits can progress as fast as this patient's did (weakness to sensory level to bowel/bladder loss within about three hours). Classic triad: back pain + fever + progressive neurologic deficit. Risk factors include IV drug use, diabetes, recent spinal procedure/instrumentation, and a skin or soft-tissue infection source (as fits a Staph. aureus abscess).

Case 3

Skydiving Instructor with Midthoracic Pain → Incidental Syrinx

Vignette

A 30-year-old owner of a skydiving school presented with midthoracic pain. He had performed more than 1,500 jumps without apparent injury. There were no abnormal physical findings. An MRI was obtained.

Sagittal MRIAn incidentally discovered syrinx (fluid-filled cavity within the cord), found while imaging for unrelated midthoracic pain.
💡 Teaching point

This case exists to make one point stick: syrinx size doesn't have to match symptom severity. A completely asymptomatic, neurologically-normal patient can harbor a syrinx found only because he was imaged for something else. Contrast this with Case 4, where a syrinx of similar type produces a dramatic, disabling clinical picture — the difference is usually location, rate of expansion, and which tracts/nuclei the cavity abuts, not just size.

Syrinxes are frequently associated with Chiari I malformation, prior trauma, or an intramedullary tumor, but many are idiopathic — and some, like this one, are simply incidental.

Case 4

Progressive Arm Wasting, Dysphonia, Dysphagia → Syringobulbia

Vignette

A 24-year-old man had a three-year history of progressive muscle wasting and sensory loss in his arms, dysphonia, and dysphagia. Over the previous five months he had had several painless burns on his hands. He had no history of cranial or cervical trauma.

Exam: marked atrophy of the right deltoid, biceps, and upper trapezius, and of the hypothenar eminence and dorsal interossei of the right hand. Biceps, triceps, and brachioradialis reflexes were bilaterally absent. Pain and heat sensation were lost in both arms, over the right side of the face, and over the chest/upper back — but touch and pressure perception were preserved. Gait was normal.

On follow-up exam: hypalgesia in the perioral skin on the left side of the face, and a decreased right corneal reflex.

🧠 Localizing the pattern

Painless burns + preserved touch but lost pain/temperature = dissociated sensory loss — the signature of a central cord process. A syrinx expands from the central canal outward, and the first fibers it interrupts are the pain/temperature fibers crossing through the ventral (anterior) white commissure just anterior to the canal — while the dorsal columns (touch, proprioception, running peripherally in the cord) are spared until much later. The bilateral, "cape-like" distribution over the arms/shoulders/upper back reflects the segments where the cavity has expanded.

🧠 Why the face and swallowing are involved

This patient also has dysphonia, dysphagia, facial hypalgesia, and a diminished corneal reflex — the cavity has extended rostrally from the cervical cord into the lower brainstem (syringobulbia). Within the medulla, the same interruption pattern applies to the descending spinal trigeminal tract/nucleus (facial pain/temperature, mapped like a dermatome onto the nucleus — the more caudal the fibers, the more peripheral/posterior the face territory they carry), which explains the facial sensory change and the blunted corneal reflex. Involvement near the nucleus ambiguus region explains the voice change and swallowing difficulty.

Imaging

T1-weighted MRI of the cervical spine (without gadolinium) demonstrated a cavitation extending along the length of the cervical cord, with similar cavitation seen in the dorsal (upper thoracic) cord on a separate sequence. A cervical syringotomy was performed; on follow-up the sensory loss and muscle wasting were unchanged, but the dysphonia and dysphagia had improved, with no further deterioration.

Sagittal MRI (2 panels)Panel A: cervical cord cavitation. Panel B: dorsal (upper thoracic) cord cavitation, same syrinx.
Additional ViewFurther imaging of the syrinx cavity along the cord.

Histology — Why Sensation Splits the Way It Does

Cross-SectionA large central cavity has destroyed the central gray matter and the decussating spinothalamic fibers passing through the ventral white commissure, while the peripherally-located dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts remain relatively intact.
Histology, Level 2Additional histologic section through the syrinx at another cord level, showing the cavity's variable size along its length.
Histology, Level 3Further section illustrating how the cavity's shape and extent change craniocaudally.
FindingTract/StructureWhy
Painless burns, dissociated pain/temp lossDecussating spinothalamic fibers (ventral white commissure)First fibers interrupted by central cavity expansion
Preserved touch/proprioceptionDorsal columnsPeripherally located — spared until late/large cavities
Arm/hand muscle wasting, absent reflexesAnterior horn cellsAnterior horns sit adjacent to the central canal — early involvement
Facial hypalgesia, blunted corneal reflexSpinal trigeminal nucleus/tractSyrinx extension into the medulla (syringobulbia)
Dysphonia, dysphagiaNucleus ambiguus regionBulbar extension affecting motor fibers of CN IX/X
Case 5

Fatal Tobogganing Injury → Wallerian Degeneration

Vignette

A 22-year-old female suffered a traumatic spinal cord injury while tobogganing. She survived the injury by two weeks. At autopsy, the spinal cord was removed, sectioned, and stained with a myelin stain.

A myelin stain lets you see degeneration directly: intact, myelinated tracts stain darkly, while a tract that has lost its axons and myelin stains pale. Two weeks is enough time for degeneration to be well underway, which is exactly why this specimen is a good teaching case.

The Underlying Principle: What Happens When an Axon Is Cut

From lecture discussion

Cutting an axon does two separate things to the neuron, and they matter clinically in opposite directions. The cell body reacts to the injury by dispersing its rough ER to ramp up protein synthesis for repair — since it's the ER that normally takes up most histologic stains, this dispersal makes the cell body look pale ("chromatolysis," literally losing its stainable substance). While reacting this way, the cell body can still keep the axon alive up to the cut. But past the cut, the distal axon segment is disconnected from the cell body's protein and energy supply — it can't survive, and it degenerates. This is Wallerian (anterograde) degeneration: it always proceeds away from the cell body, through the segment of axon that has lost its cell body connection.

Axon transected→ Segment still attached to cell body: survives→ Segment cut off from cell body: degenerates (Wallerian)

Applying This to a Cord Transection

Sensory (ascending) and motor (descending) systems have their cell bodies at opposite ends, so a single transection produces degeneration in opposite directions for each system:

Sensory / ascending tracts

Cell bodies (dorsal root ganglia) sit below the lesion. The axon segment running from the cell body up to the cut survives; everything from the cut upward to the brain is disconnected and degenerates. → Degeneration ascends from the lesion toward the brain, but the functional deficit is a loss below the level (the brain can no longer be reached).

Motor / descending tracts

Cell bodies (upper motor neurons) sit above the lesion, in the brain. The segment from the cortex down to the cut survives; everything from the cut downward is disconnected and degenerates. → Degeneration descends from the lesion toward the sacrum, and everything below the lesion cannot be driven by the cortex.

💡 Net effect

Above the level of a complete transection: motor is preserved (upper motor neuron cell bodies are intact and above the cut), but sensory information from below can no longer ascend past the cut. Below the level: sensation from below can still be generated locally, but none of it — and no voluntary motor command — can cross the transected segment. Everything above the lesion "works" on its own; everything below is functionally isolated.

The Specimen

Cervical SectionMyelin-stained cross-section above the injury level. Pale (degenerated) staining is seen in the ascending sensory tracts that were disconnected from the brain by the lesion below.
Lumbar SectionMyelin-stained cross-section below the injury level. Pale staining here is seen in the descending motor tracts, disconnected from their cortical cell bodies above.
Neuron Injury ResponseSchematic of a single axotomized neuron: anterograde (Wallerian) degeneration distal to the cut vs. the retrograde chromatolytic reaction in the cell body proximal to it.
Ascending vs. Descending DegenerationSensory (posterior fasciculus, spinocerebellar, lateral spinothalamic) tracts degenerate above the transection; motor (lateral & anterior corticospinal) tracts degenerate below it.
🎯 Exam framing

If you're handed a myelin-stained cross-section and asked "is this above or below the lesion, and which tracts are pale?" — work backward from this rule: pale dorsal/lateral sensory columns = section is above the lesion; pale corticospinal tracts = section is below the lesion.

Case 6

Near-Drowning with Hyperextended Neck → Vertebral Artery Dissection & Wallenberg Syndrome

Vignette

A woman was swimming at a beach in Maine when she was knocked down by a wave and hyperextended her neck; it took three people to pull her from the water. She later told her family physician that she felt dizzy, felt unsafe walking on the floor, and felt like she was choking — but denied ever actually falling or choking.

She had an extensive prior psychiatric and somatic history (multiple physicians, depression, an old-generation antidepressant), and her new complaints were initially dismissed against that background.

⚠️ Anchoring bias, corrected

A thick psychiatric chart made her new neurologic symptoms easy to write off. A neurologist who actually examined her found mild but real findings: sensory asymmetry between the two sides of her face, and a funny sensation in one arm. These were intermittent — and intermittent, fluctuating deficits after a neck hyperextension injury should raise concern for arterial dissection, not be dismissed as psychiatric.

The Exam Finding That Cracked the Case

On oral exam, the neurologist looked into the pharynx/larynx and found food particles and saliva pooled in the piriform recess on one side — meaning that side wasn't being actively cleared ("milked") by the pharyngeal muscles. That single finding was enough to justify imaging.

Neck hyperextension in the surf→ Vertebral artery intimal tear→ Intermittent flap occlusion→ Eventual clot / vessel occlusion

Imaging Work-Up

Angiographic StudyContrast injected into the posterior circulation. The vertebral artery fills, then stops abruptly — the expected cascade of posterior fossa vessels distal to that point is essentially absent.
Sagittal MRIMidline sagittal view for orientation to the brainstem and posterior fossa.
Axial, Level 1Axial section through the brainstem/posterior fossa.
Axial, Level 2Sequential axial section through the medulla, near the fourth ventricle.
Axial, Level 3Sequential axial section, slightly more rostral.
Axial, Level 4Different pulse sequence comparing the flow void of the two vertebral arteries — one shows normal flow, the other shows an occlusive plug.
Axial, Level 5Further comparison section.

Localizing the Lesion: Lateral Medulla

Lateral Medulla, LabeledCross-section through the rostral medulla at the level of the fourth ventricle, with the descending spinal trigeminal tract/nucleus, spinothalamic tract, inferior cerebellar peduncle, nucleus ambiguus, and vestibular nuclei all packed into the same small territory supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)/vertebral artery.
Vertebrobasilar SystemThe two vertebral arteries join to form the single basilar artery — one of the few places in the body where two large vessels merge into one — which then divides into the paired posterior cerebral arteries.
Vertebral Artery CourseCourse of the vertebral artery from its origin off the subclavian artery, through the transverse foramina, to its junction with the basilar artery.
Rostral Medulla PerfusionContrast-injected specimen showing the fine perforating branches supplying the rostral medulla. A single occluded perforator can infarct a small, specific territory while neighboring overlapping branches keep the rest of the region perfused — explaining why this patient had only a partial syndrome.

Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome — Full Syndrome vs. This Patient's Fragment

Textbook lateral medullary syndrome results from occlusion of the vertebral artery or PICA and knocks out a cluster of structures packed into the dorsolateral medulla. This patient's story is a good reminder that in practice you usually see a partial/fragmentary version, not the full textbook picture:

StructureDeficitThis Patient
Spinal trigeminal nucleus/tractIpsilateral facial pain/temperature lossOnly mild facial sensory asymmetry — territory just spared full analgesia
Lateral spinothalamic tractContralateral body pain/temperature lossFunny sensation in one arm
Nucleus ambiguusIpsilateral palatal/pharyngeal/laryngeal weakness → dysphagia, dysphonia, hoarsenessPooling of secretions in the piriform recess; voice change noticed by friends
Vestibular nucleiVertigo, nystagmusFelt dizzy, unsteady on shiny/smooth floors
Inferior cerebellar peduncleIpsilateral limb/gait ataxiaFelt unsteady but did not actually fall
Descending sympathetic fibersIpsilateral Horner's syndromeNot reported in this case
🎯 Board term

Lateral medullary syndrome is also called Wallenberg syndrome — worth knowing by name. It classically follows vertebral artery or PICA occlusion/dissection.

Why Wasn't She Dead? And Why Was the Infarct So Small?

Two separate protective factors explain her limited deficit:

Redundant supply — the other vertebral artery

The two vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery. With one vertebral artery occluded, the contralateral vertebral artery can still perfuse the basilar system from below, and can partially supply the affected side retrograde — minimizing the territory actually infarcted.

Overlapping perforator branches

The rostral medulla is fed by numerous small, overlapping perforating branches. Losing one perforator knocks out only its unique territory; neighboring branches continue to cover the surrounding tissue, which is why her deficit was a fragment of the full syndrome rather than the whole picture.

Management Principle

⚠️ Don't dislodge the clot

By the time she was diagnosed, she was well outside any window for clot-dissolving therapy, and the greater danger was dislodging an already-organizing clot rather than dissolving it. Management centered on minimizing neck movement to let the clot organize/canalize and re-establish flow over time. If a fragment of that clot were to embolize distally, it would travel through the vertebral artery into the basilar artery, and at the top of the basilar it could enter either (or both) posterior cerebral artery — producing a thalamic infarct, an occipital (visual cortex) infarct, or both. That downstream event would be a far larger, more dangerous stroke than the original lateral medullary injury.
